Tell everyone that rest is only for those who did less work
Invite them to come apart to a quiet place and rest a while
Praise the skipped meals as proof of true commitment
explanation: In Mark 6:31 Jesus told his busy disciples, "Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while," because "they had no leisure so much as to eat."
hint: Consider what Jesus told his disciples when they had no leisure even to eat.

prompt: You're offered a promotion with much higher pay, but it would mean constant stress, long hours, and little peace at home. Your current role pays less but leaves room for a calm life. What does Ecclesiastes 4:6 counsel here?
options: Both hands full is always better, whatever the vexation
A handful with quietness is better than both hands full with travail and vexation of spirit
Quietness only matters once you have accumulated plenty
Travail is the surest path to a peaceful spirit
explanation: Ecclesiastes 4:6 says, "Better is an handful with quietness, than both the hands full with travail and vexation of spirit," valuing peace above more gain gotten with turmoil.
hint: The verse compares one handful with two, and weighs what comes with each.

prompt: You've begun working nights and weekends purely to grow your investments, constantly watching market charts and neglecting friendships. A coworker urges you to chase wealth even harder. Which response best reflects the teaching of Proverbs 23:4-5?
options: Set your eyes firmly on riches, since they are the most lasting thing
Trust your own cleverness to make sure your riches never leave
Labour all the harder, because wealth stays with those who pursue it
Labour not to be rich, remembering that riches make themselves wings and fly away
explanation: Proverbs 23:4-5 warns, "Labour not to be rich: cease from thine own wisdom," because "riches certainly make themselves wings; they fly away as an eagle toward heaven."
hint: Consider what the proverb says about how lasting riches are, and about relying on your own wisdom to hold onto them.

prompt: Your teenage nephew is living with you for a year, and you are tempted to leave his character and habits for 'life to sort out later.' You wonder whether patient guidance now really matters. Which response best reflects the teaching of Proverbs 22:6?
options: Assume children will find their own way and that early guidance makes little lasting difference
Wait until he is an adult before trying to shape his habits or values
Leave all guidance to his school, since home life has little effect on character
Take time now to train him in the right way, trusting that early formation tends to last into later life
explanation: Proverbs 22:6 says to 'Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it,' so diligent guidance in youth has lasting value.
hint: Think about what this verse says happens 'when he is old.'

prompt: Your elderly parents call often, and after a stressful week you are tempted to ignore them and speak dismissively about them to friends. You want to respond rightly. What does Exodus 20:12 counsel here?
options: Honour your father and mother, treating them with respect and regard even when it is inconvenient
Honour your parents only if they have earned it by agreeing with your choices
Keep your distance, since adult children owe their parents nothing further
Speak respectfully to their faces but freely mock them to others
explanation: Exodus 20:12 commands, 'Honour thy father and thy mother,' attaching a promise of long days to the command, with no condition about convenience.
hint: This is one of the Ten Commandments, and the first word of it is a verb about respect.

prompt: At a community meeting, an elderly man with white hair slowly makes his way to the front, and some younger attendees roll their eyes and keep their seats. You consider how to respond. Which response best reflects the teaching of Leviticus 19:32?
options: Ignore him, since respect should be based only on someone's position or wealth
Rise and show him honour, treating age itself with respect as an act of reverence toward God
Join the others in quietly laughing at how slow he is
Offer respect only if he proves he is more qualified than the younger speakers
explanation: Leviticus 19:32 says, 'Thou shalt rise up before the hoary head, and honour the face of the old man, and fear thy God,' tying respect for the aged to reverence for the LORD.
hint: The verse describes a physical action of respect toward grey hair.

prompt: Your mother, now in her eighties, offers advice about a family matter. Friends say her views are outdated and you should simply tune her out because of her age. What does Proverbs 23:22 counsel here?
options: Stop consulting parents once you have your own household
Listen politely only to your father, since the verse concerns fathers alone
Treat her age as a reason to dismiss her opinions
Listen to your parents and do not despise your mother because she has grown old
explanation: Proverbs 23:22 says, 'Hearken unto thy father that begat thee, and despise not thy mother when she is old,' forbidding contempt for an aging parent.
hint: Notice what the verse says about a mother's age.

prompt: An older volunteer at your organisation has made a real mistake, and you need to address it. A colleague suggests confronting him sharply in front of everyone so he learns his lesson. Which response best reflects the teaching of 1 Timothy 5:1-2?
options: Rebuke him harshly, since age gives no special claim to gentle treatment
Never mention the problem at all, even if it continues
Approach him respectfully and appeal to him as you would to your own father
Ask a younger staff member to scold him publicly so you are not involved
explanation: 1 Timothy 5:1 says, 'Rebuke not an elder, but intreat him as a father,' calling for respectful appeal rather than harsh rebuke, and goes on to treat others as family 'with all purity.'
hint: The passage compares how to treat older and younger people to members of a family.

prompt: Your child keeps failing to finish chores, and you are frustrated. You are tempted to respond with constant belittling and harsh outbursts to 'toughen them up.' Which response best reflects the teaching of Ephesians 6:4?
options: Avoid needlessly provoking them to anger, and instead raise them with patient instruction and godly correction
Use sarcasm and ridicule, since shame is the quickest way to change behaviour
Give up on correction entirely so the child never feels upset
Let the child raise themselves, since instruction is the church's job alone
keywords: provoke not your children to wrath
explanation: Ephesians 6:4 tells fathers to 'provoke not your children to wrath: but bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord,' which rules out both exasperating harshness and abandoning correction.
hint: The verse contains both a warning and a positive instruction for parents.

prompt: Your aging father needs some financial help. You are tempted to tell him your money is already pledged to a religious cause, so you are excused from helping him, even though you could do both. In light of Mark 7:10-13, what does Scripture counsel here?
options: A religious pledge rightly cancels any duty to help your parents
Declaring resources set apart as a gift is a wise way to avoid family obligations
Do not use a religious vow as an excuse to neglect your parents, because that makes God's command to honour them of none effect
Honouring parents means only speaking kindly, not practical help
explanation: In Mark 7:10-13 Jesus rebukes those who declared their resources 'Corban' so they need do nothing for father or mother, saying this made 'the word of God of none effect through your tradition.'
hint: Jesus criticised a tradition that used a 'gift' to God as a loophole.

prompt: You are the youngest person newly appointed to lead a team, and several older members quietly doubt you because of your age. You wonder how to respond. Which response best reflects the teaching of 1 Timothy 4:12?
options: Demand respect forcefully and remind them often that you are in charge
Become an example in your speech, conduct, love, spirit, faith and purity so your youth gives no cause for contempt
Step aside, since young people should never hold responsibility
Match their attitude by dismissing the older members' contributions
explanation: 1 Timothy 4:12 says, 'Let no man despise thy youth; but be thou an example of the believers, in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity,' answering doubts through godly example rather than force.
hint: The verse lists areas of life where a young person should set a pattern.

prompt: Elkanah went up yearly to worship and sacrifice to the LORD at the town marked on the map, where Eli's sons served as priests. Which town is it?
explanation: Elkanah went up yearly to sacrifice to the LORD of hosts in Shiloh, where Hophni and Phinehas, the sons of Eli, were priests (1 Samuel 1:3).
hint: The tabernacle stood here in the days of Eli, in the hill country of Ephraim.

prompt: David and his men went up against the Jebusites and took the stronghold of Zion, the city of David. Which marker shows Jerusalem?
explanation: The king and his men went to Jerusalem against the Jebusites, and David took the stronghold of Zion, the city of David (2 Samuel 5:6-7).
hint: Look in the hill country west of the northern end of the Salt Sea.

prompt: The Philistine champion Goliath, who challenged Israel's army, came from Gath. Which marker shows Gath?
explanation: Goliath, the champion of the Philistines, was 'of Gath' (1 Samuel 17:4).
hint: It was one of the Philistine cities, in the lowlands toward the coastal plain.

prompt: After Saul died in battle, the Philistines fastened his body to the wall of the city marked on the map. Which city is it?
explanation: The Philistines put Saul's armour in the house of Ashtaroth and fastened his body to the wall of Beth-shan (1 Samuel 31:10).
hint: This city lies where the Jezreel valley opens toward the Jordan, not far from Mount Gilboa.

prompt: Elisha passed through Shunem, where a great woman constrained him to eat bread. Which marker shows Shunem?
explanation: Elisha passed to Shunem, where a great woman constrained him to eat bread (2 Kings 4:8).
hint: It sits in the north, overlooking the Jezreel valley.

prompt: In the days of Deborah, the LORD sold Israel into the hand of Jabin king of Canaan, who reigned in the city marked on the map. Which city is it?
explanation: Jabin king of Canaan reigned in Hazor, and the captain of his host was Sisera (Judges 4:2).
hint: This great Canaanite city lay in upper Galilee, north of the Sea of Galilee.

prompt: Manoah, the father of Samson, was a man of the town marked on the map. Which town is it?
explanation: There was a certain man of Zorah, of the family of the Danites, whose name was Manoah (Judges 13:2).
hint: This town of the Danites lay in the lowland hills west of Jerusalem.

prompt: David and his men fought the Philistines and saved the inhabitants of Keilah. Which marker shows Keilah?
explanation: David and his men went to Keilah, fought with the Philistines, and saved the inhabitants of Keilah (1 Samuel 23:5).
hint: It lay in the territory of Judah, in the lowlands northwest of Hebron.

prompt: While David tarried at Jerusalem, Joab and Israel's army destroyed the children of Ammon and besieged Rabbah. Which marker shows Rabbah?
explanation: David sent Joab and all Israel, and they destroyed the children of Ammon and besieged Rabbah, while David tarried still at Jerusalem (2 Samuel 11:1).
hint: The Ammonite royal city lay east of the Jordan.

prompt: Paul told the chief captain in Jerusalem that he was a Jew of the city marked on the map, 'a city in Cilicia.' Which city is it?
explanation: Paul said, 'I am a man which am a Jew of Tarsus, a city in Cilicia, a citizen of no mean city' (Acts 21:39).
hint: Saul is often identified by this hometown.

prompt: While Paul was at Troas, a vision of a man of Macedonia called him to come over and help. Which marker shows Troas?
explanation: Passing by Mysia, Paul's company came down to Troas, where a vision of a man of Macedonia appeared to Paul in the night (Acts 16:8-9).
hint: Look for a port in northwest Asia Minor facing Macedonia across the sea.

prompt: Hurrying toward Jerusalem, Paul stopped at the place marked on the map and sent for the elders of the church at Ephesus. Which place is it?
explanation: 'And from Miletus he sent to Ephesus, and called the elders of the church' (Acts 20:17).
hint: It is a coastal city south of Ephesus.

prompt: Laodicea was one of the seven churches in Asia to which John was told to send what he saw. Which marker shows Laodicea?
explanation: John was told to send the book 'unto the seven churches which are in Asia,' ending with Laodicea (Revelation 1:11).
hint: The seven churches were in the province of Asia, in the west of Asia Minor.

prompt: Paul and Barnabas went together into the synagogue of the Jews in the city marked on the map, and a great multitude believed. Which city is it?
explanation: In Iconium Paul and Barnabas went into the synagogue and so spake that a great multitude of Jews and Greeks believed (Acts 14:1).
hint: It lies inland in south-central Asia Minor, visited before Lystra and Derbe.

prompt: After being stoned at Lystra, Paul departed the next day with Barnabas to Derbe and preached there. Which marker shows Derbe?
explanation: After Paul was stoned at Lystra, 'the next day he departed with Barnabas to Derbe' and preached the gospel to that city (Acts 14:19-21).
hint: It is in inland Asia Minor, not far from Lystra.

prompt: Sent forth by the Holy Ghost, Barnabas and Saul went down to Seleucia and sailed to the island marked on the map. Which island is it?
explanation: Being sent forth by the Holy Ghost, they 'departed unto Seleucia; and from thence they sailed to Cyprus' (Acts 13:4).
hint: It is the large island in the eastern corner of the Mediterranean.

prompt: Passing through Amphipolis and Apollonia, Paul came to Thessalonica, where there was a synagogue of the Jews. Which marker shows Thessalonica?
explanation: Paul and Silas 'came to Thessalonica, where was a synagogue of the Jews' (Acts 17:1).
hint: Look in Macedonia, in northern Greece.

prompt: Cornelius, a centurion of the Italian band, lived in Caesarea. Which marker shows Caesarea?
explanation: 'There was a certain man in Caesarea called Cornelius, a centurion of the band called the Italian band' (Acts 10:1).
hint: It is a port on the coast of the Holy Land.

prompt: Paul wrote to Titus that he had left him on the island marked on the map to set things in order and ordain elders in every city. Which island is it?
explanation: Paul told Titus, 'For this cause left I thee in Crete,' to set in order the things wanting and ordain elders (Titus 1:4-5).
hint: It is a long island south of the Greek mainland.

clue: Camp report: the visitors' sacks are old, their wine bottles torn and bound up, their shoes patched, and all their bread dry and mouldy. Word has it they had heard what Joshua did to Jericho and Ai.
prompt: According to the text, the inhabitants of which town planned this disguise?
options: Gibeon
Jericho
Ai
Gilgal
explanation: Joshua 9:3-5 says the inhabitants of Gibeon 'did work wilily' and came with old sacks, old shoes and mouldy bread. Jericho and Ai were the cities Joshua had already conquered, and Gilgal was Israel's camp (Joshua 9:6).
hint: The plotters had heard about Jericho and Ai, so they were not from either of those cities.

clue: Witness statement: the travellers pointed to their dry bread and told the Israelites a story about when it had been packed.
prompt: What did the travellers claim about their bread?
options: They took it hot out of their houses on the day they set out
They bought it at a market in Gilgal
They received it as a gift from the king of Ai
They baked it fresh that morning
explanation: In Joshua 9:12-13 the travellers said they took the bread hot from their houses when they set out, and that it had become dry and mouldy, their bottles torn and clothes worn 'by reason of the very long journey.'
hint: They used the bread to suggest how long they had been travelling.

clue: Procedure note: the Israelite men examined the visitors' food, and Joshua and the princes swore an oath of peace. One important step was left out.
prompt: What did the men of Israel fail to do before making the league?
options: They asked not counsel at the mouth of the LORD
They did not taste the visitors' food
They did not let the princes swear
They did not let Joshua make peace
explanation: Joshua 9:14 says the men took of their victuals 'and asked not counsel at the mouth of the LORD.' Verse 15 shows Joshua made peace and the princes swore, so the other options contradict the text.
hint: They checked the evidence with their own eyes but did not seek guidance from someone else.

clue: Follow-up report: just three days after the treaty, Israel received news about the strangers and marched to their cities, arriving on the third day.
prompt: What did Israel discover about the travellers?
options: They were neighbours who dwelt among them
They lived beyond the great sea
They came from Egypt
They were Israelites from another tribe
explanation: Joshua 9:16 says Israel heard 'that they were their neighbours, and that they dwelt among them,' and verse 17 names their cities: Gibeon, Chephirah, Beeroth and Kirjathjearim.
hint: The 'very long journey' turned out to be much shorter than claimed.

clue: Final interrogation: Joshua asked, 'Wherefore have ye beguiled us?' The Gibeonites gave their reason and placed themselves in his hand.
prompt: Case solved: what really happened, and how did it end?
options: The Gibeonites, sore afraid for their lives, pretended to come from far away; they were spared but made hewers of wood and drawers of water
The Gibeonites were truly from a far country and became Israel's honoured allies
The men of Ai disguised themselves, and Joshua destroyed them
The Gibeonites stole Israel's bread and were driven out of the land
explanation: In Joshua 9:24 the Gibeonites said they 'were sore afraid of our lives' and so 'have done this thing.' Joshua 9:26-27 says he delivered them from being slain and made them hewers of wood and drawers of water for the congregation and the altar of the LORD.
hint: Their lives were spared because of the oath, but their deception had a lasting consequence.

clue: Witness report: Jesus and his disciples passed a man blind since birth, and the disciples asked their Master a pointed question about blame.
prompt: According to Jesus, why was this man born blind?
options: Because his parents had sinned
Because the man himself had sinned
So that the works of God should be made manifest in him
Because he had broken the sabbath
explanation: Jesus answered that neither the man nor his parents had sinned, but that the works of God should be made manifest in him (John 9:3).
hint: Jesus rejected both options the disciples suggested.

clue: Physical evidence: traces of clay made with spittle were applied to the man's eyes, and he was given instructions to go somewhere.
prompt: Where was the man told to go and wash?
options: The river Jordan
The pool of Siloam
The pool of Bethesda
The temple laver
explanation: Jesus anointed the man's eyes with clay and told him, 'Go, wash in the pool of Siloam'; he washed and came seeing (John 9:6-7).
hint: The name of this pool is interpreted as 'Sent.'

clue: Pharisee testimony: 'This man is not of God,' some of them said of the healer, pointing to the day on which the clay was made.
prompt: On what day did Jesus make the clay and open the man's eyes?
options: The day of Pentecost
The first day of the week
The sabbath day
The day of atonement
explanation: It was the sabbath day when Jesus made the clay, and some Pharisees said he was not of God because he kept not the sabbath day (John 9:14,16).
hint: Their objection concerned a weekly day of rest.

clue: Statement of the parents: 'We know that this is our son, and that he was born blind... he is of age; ask him.'
prompt: Why did the man's parents refuse to say how their son received his sight?
options: They feared the Jews, who had agreed to put out of the synagogue anyone who confessed Jesus was Christ
They had not seen their son in many years
They believed he had been healed by a physician
They were angry with their son
explanation: His parents spoke this way because they feared the Jews, who had agreed that anyone confessing Jesus as Christ would be put out of the synagogue (John 9:22).
hint: Consider what the text says would happen to anyone who made a certain confession.

clue: Final report: after the man was cast out, Jesus found him and asked, 'Dost thou believe on the Son of God?'
prompt: What really happened when Jesus revealed himself to the healed man?
options: The man went away doubting
The man returned to the Pharisees to accuse Jesus
The man said, 'Lord, I believe,' and worshipped him
The man asked for another sign before believing
explanation: When Jesus said, 'it is he that talketh with thee,' the man replied, 'Lord, I believe,' and he worshipped him (John 9:37-38).
hint: The man's answer was short and his response was immediate.

clue: Witness report: The patriarch is old and his eyes are dim. He was heard sending his elder son out to the field with quiver and bow, promising a blessing afterward.
prompt: What did Isaac ask Esau to bring him before giving the blessing?
options: Venison made into savoury meat
A lamb from the flock for a sacrifice
Bread and wine from the city
Water from a well in the wilderness
explanation: Isaac told Esau to take his weapons, hunt venison, and make savoury meat, 'that my soul may bless thee before I die' (Genesis 27:3-4).
hint: Think of what a hunter brings home from the field.

clue: Overheard conversation: Someone in the household heard Isaac's instructions to Esau and quickly gave Jacob a set of instructions of her own.
prompt: What did Rebekah tell Jacob to fetch from the flock?
options: Two good kids of the goats
A young bullock
Seven ewe lambs
A pair of turtledoves
keywords: two good kids of the goats
explanation: Rebekah told Jacob to fetch 'two good kids of the goats' so she could make savoury meat for Isaac (Genesis 27:9).
hint: The animals came from the flock and their skins would prove useful later.

clue: Physical evidence: Jacob had worried that his father would feel him, since his brother was hairy and he was smooth. The garments and some animal skins were later found to have been used.
prompt: How was Jacob disguised before going in to Isaac?
options: He wore Esau's goodly raiment and goat skins on his hands and neck
He wore a veil over his face
He covered himself with sackcloth and ashes
He wore a priest's linen ephod
explanation: Rebekah put Esau's goodly raiment on Jacob and put the skins of the kids of the goats on his hands and the smooth of his neck (Genesis 27:15-16).
hint: The disguise targeted Isaac's sense of touch and borrowed from the elder brother's wardrobe.

clue: Statement from the tent: After feeling his son, the blind father voiced a doubt about what he heard compared with what he felt.
prompt: What did Isaac say when he felt Jacob?
options: The voice is Jacob's voice, but the hands are the hands of Esau
The smell is not the smell of my son
Thou art too young to be Esau
Thy meat is not as I love it
explanation: Isaac felt him and said, 'The voice is Jacob's voice, but the hands are the hands of Esau,' and he discerned him not (Genesis 27:22-23).
hint: One sense told Isaac the truth while another was deceived.

clue: Final testimony: When the true elder son arrived from hunting, Isaac trembled very exceedingly and explained to him what had happened.
prompt: According to Isaac's explanation to Esau, who had taken the blessing?
options: Jacob, his brother, who came with subtilty
A servant who stole Esau's garments
Rebekah, who asked for it herself
No one; Isaac had not yet blessed anyone
explanation: Isaac told Esau, 'Thy brother came with subtilty, and hath taken away thy blessing' (Genesis 27:35).
hint: Isaac named the culprit by his relation to Esau.

clue: Witness statement from Naaman's company: 'Our master stood before the prophet and begged him to accept a gift. The prophet swore an oath by the LORD and would not budge.'
prompt: How did Elisha respond when Naaman urged him to take a blessing (a gift)?
options: He refused, saying, 'As the LORD liveth, before whom I stand, I will receive none.'
He accepted half of the gift for the sons of the prophets.
He told Naaman to send the gift to the king of Israel.
He accepted only the changes of garments.
explanation: Naaman asked Elisha to take a blessing, but Elisha swore he would receive none and refused even when urged (2 Kings 5:15-16).
hint: Pay attention to the oath the prophet swore.

clue: Report from the road: 'A man came running after the chariot. Naaman stepped down to meet him and asked, Is all well? The runner said his master had sent him.'
prompt: What reason did Gehazi give Naaman for coming after him?
options: Elisha had changed his mind and wanted the whole gift.
Two young men of the sons of the prophets had come from mount Ephraim and needed a talent of silver and two changes of garments.
The king of Israel demanded payment for the healing.
Naaman had left his mules' burden of earth behind.
explanation: Gehazi claimed his master had sent him because two young men of the sons of the prophets had arrived from mount Ephraim, and he asked for a talent of silver and two changes of garments (2 Kings 5:22).
hint: The runner mentioned visitors from a hill country region.

clue: Inventory note: 'Bound in two bags and carried by two of Naaman's servants, along with two changes of garments.'
prompt: How much silver did Naaman actually give?
options: One talent of silver
Ten talents of silver
Two talents of silver
Six thousand pieces of gold
explanation: Naaman said, 'Be content, take two talents,' and bound two talents of silver in two bags with two changes of garments (2 Kings 5:23).
hint: Naaman gave more than was requested; count the bags.

clue: Observation at the tower: 'Two of Naaman's servants carried the bags ahead of the man, then were sent on their way.'
prompt: What did Gehazi do with the silver and garments when he came to the tower?
options: He gave them to the two young men from mount Ephraim.
He took them from the servants' hands and bestowed them in the house, then let the men go.
He brought them openly to Elisha.
He buried them beside the Jordan.
explanation: At the tower Gehazi took the goods from the servants, bestowed them in the house, and sent the men away (2 Kings 5:24).
hint: Look at where he stopped and where the goods were put.

clue: Final interview: Elisha asked, 'Whence comest thou, Gehazi?' The servant answered that he had gone nowhere, but the prophet replied that his own heart had gone with Gehazi.
prompt: What really happened when Gehazi stood before Elisha?
options: Gehazi confessed, and Elisha forgave him without consequence.
Elisha believed Gehazi, and the matter was forgotten.
Gehazi lied, saying 'Thy servant went no whither'; Elisha revealed he knew, and Naaman's leprosy came upon Gehazi.
Naaman returned to reclaim the silver, and Gehazi fled.
explanation: Gehazi claimed, 'Thy servant went no whither,' but Elisha answered, 'Went not mine heart with thee?' He pronounced that Naaman's leprosy would cleave to Gehazi, and Gehazi went out a leper as white as snow (2 Kings 5:25-27).
hint: Compare Gehazi's answer with what Elisha said he already knew.

clue: Background report: Israel did evil in the sight of the LORD, and a foreign ruler allied with Ammon and Amalek seized the city of palm trees.
prompt: Who was the ruler oppressing Israel, and for how long did Israel serve him?
options: Eglon the king of Moab, for eighteen years
Jabin king of Canaan, for twenty years
Eglon the king of Ammon, for seven years
Cushanrishathaim of Mesopotamia, for forty years
explanation: The LORD strengthened Eglon the king of Moab against Israel, and the children of Israel served him eighteen years (Judges 3:12-14).
hint: Ammon and Amalek were his allies, not his own kingdom.

clue: Suspect profile: a Benjamite, the son of Gera, sent by Israel to carry a present to the king. He prepared a weapon before the journey.
prompt: Where did Ehud conceal the two-edged dagger he made?
options: Under his raiment upon his left thigh
Inside the present carried to the king
Under his raiment upon his right thigh
In the sleeve of his left arm
explanation: Ehud, a left-handed Benjamite, made a two-edged dagger a cubit long and girded it under his raiment upon his right thigh (Judges 3:15-16).
hint: Think about which side a left-handed man would draw from.

clue: Witness statement: after the present was delivered and the bearers sent away, the messenger turned back from the quarries by Gilgal and asked to see the king privately.
prompt: What did Ehud say to Eglon once they were alone in the summer parlour?
options: I bring tribute from the elders of Israel
I have a message from God unto thee
I come to swear peace between our peoples
I have a letter from the king of Ammon
explanation: Ehud first claimed a secret errand so the attendants went out, then in the summer parlour said, 'I have a message from God unto thee,' and Eglon arose from his seat (Judges 3:19-20).
hint: The king rose from his seat when he heard who the message was from.

clue: Scene report: the visitor left through the porch. Afterward the king's servants waited a long time outside the parlour before anyone went in.
prompt: According to the text, why did the servants delay entering the parlour?
options: Ehud had ordered them to stay outside until evening
They feared the king's anger at being disturbed at a feast
The doors were locked, and they supposed he covereth his feet in his summer chamber
They could not find anyone to open the doors until morning
explanation: Finding the parlour doors locked, the servants said, 'Surely he covereth his feet in his summer chamber,' and tarried until they were ashamed, then used a key and found their lord dead (Judges 3:24-25).
hint: The locked doors led them to assume the king wanted privacy.

clue: Final report: while the servants tarried, the messenger was already gone. A trumpet was soon heard in the mountain of Ephraim.
prompt: What was the outcome of the case after Ehud escaped?
options: Ehud escaped unto Seirath, Israel took the fords of Jordan, Moab was subdued, and the land had rest fourscore years
Ehud was captured at the quarries, but Israel later defeated Moab and had rest forty years
Ehud fled to Gilgal, Moab's army escaped across the Jordan, and the land had rest twenty years
Ehud became king over Israel and made peace with Moab for eighty years
explanation: Ehud escaped unto Seirath, rallied Israel, seized the fords of Jordan so no Moabite passed over, and Moab was subdued; the land had rest fourscore years (Judges 3:26-30).
hint: Watch the fords of Jordan, and note how many years of rest 'fourscore' means.

clue: Surveyor's note: The vineyard in question lay in Jezreel, right beside the palace of Ahab king of Samaria. The king made an offer for it.
prompt: According to Ahab's offer, what did he want to turn Naboth's vineyard into?
options: A garden of herbs
A courtyard for his chariots
A burial ground for his fathers
A threshing floor for grain
explanation: Ahab asked for the vineyard 'that I may have it for a garden of herbs, because it is near unto my house,' offering a better vineyard or its worth in money (1 Kings 21:2).
hint: Ahab gave as his reason that the vineyard was near unto his house. Think of a plot he could use close to home.

clue: Witness statement: The king came home heavy and displeased, lay on his bed, turned his face away and would eat no bread, all because of Naboth's answer.
prompt: What reason did Naboth give for refusing to give up his vineyard?
options: The price Ahab offered was too low
It was the inheritance of his fathers
He had already promised it to Jezebel
The vines were about to be harvested
explanation: Naboth said, 'The LORD forbid it me, that I should give the inheritance of my fathers unto thee,' and Ahab went home heavy and displeased (1 Kings 21:3-4).
hint: Naboth's answer was about family land, not about money.

clue: Exhibit A: Letters were delivered to the elders and nobles of Naboth's city. They bore the king's name and were sealed with the king's seal.
prompt: Who actually wrote the letters sent in Ahab's name?
options: Ahab himself
The elders of Jezreel
Jezebel
Elijah the Tishbite
explanation: After promising Ahab, 'I will give thee the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite,' Jezebel 'wrote letters in Ahab's name, and sealed them with his seal' (1 Kings 21:7-8).
hint: Look for the person who told Ahab to arise, eat bread, and let his heart be merry.

clue: Court record: A fast was proclaimed and Naboth was set on high among the people. Two men sat before him and testified in public.
prompt: What accusation did the two men of Belial bring against Naboth?
options: That he had stolen from the king's treasury
That he had moved his neighbour's landmark
That he had worshipped Baal
That he did blaspheme God and the king
explanation: The men of Belial witnessed, 'Naboth did blaspheme God and the king,' and he was carried out of the city and stoned until he died (1 Kings 21:13).
hint: The letters scripted the exact charge in advance. Compare the instruction with the testimony.

clue: Final report: As Ahab went down to take possession of the vineyard, the word of the LORD came to Elijah the Tishbite with a question for the king.
prompt: In the LORD's message through Elijah, what did He charge Ahab with?
options: Having killed, and also taken possession
Only failing to pay a fair price for the land
Breaking a treaty with the king of Syria
Refusing to proclaim a fast
explanation: The LORD sent Elijah to say, 'Hast thou killed, and also taken possession?' and declared that dogs would lick Ahab's blood where they licked Naboth's (1 Kings 21:19).
hint: The LORD's question named two things together: what happened to Naboth and what happened to the vineyard.

clue: Case file, day after the preparation: a delegation met the governor. One of them was recorded saying, 'Sir, we remember that that deceiver said... After three days I will rise again.'
prompt: Who went to Pilate, and what did they say they feared?
options: The chief priests and Pharisees, fearing the disciples would steal the body and say he was risen
The disciples, fearing the Romans would move the body
Joseph of Arimathaea, fearing robbers would damage the tomb
The elders of Galilee, fearing a riot at the feast
explanation: The chief priests and Pharisees came to Pilate asking that the sepulchre be made sure, 'lest his disciples come by night, and steal him away' (Matthew 27:62-64).
hint: Look at who 'came together unto Pilate' and the phrase beginning 'lest his disciples...'

clue: Governor's reply on record: 'Ye have a watch: go your way, make it as sure as ye can.' Those who asked then went to the sepulchre to act on his word.
prompt: What two measures were taken to secure the sepulchre?
options: The stone was sealed and a watch was set
The door was bricked up and the key given to Pilate
The body was moved and the tomb left empty
A second stone was added and the disciples were arrested
explanation: They went and made the sepulchre sure, 'sealing the stone, and setting a watch' (Matthew 27:65-66).
hint: The final verse names two actions joined by 'and'.

clue: Early on the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to see the sepulchre. There was a great earthquake, and the stone was no longer in the door.
prompt: According to the text, who rolled back the stone, and what happened to the keepers?
options: The angel of the Lord rolled it back, and the keepers shook and became as dead men
The disciples rolled it back while the keepers slept
The women rolled it back, and the keepers fled to Pilate
The earthquake moved it, and the keepers arrested the women
explanation: The angel of the Lord descended, rolled back the stone and sat upon it, and 'for fear of him the keepers did shake, and became as dead men' (Matthew 28:2-4).
hint: Check who 'descended from heaven' and how the keepers reacted 'for fear of him'.

clue: Statement attributed to the figure at the tomb, addressed to the women: 'Fear not ye.' He then invited them to look at a certain place.
prompt: What did the angel tell the women about Jesus?
options: He is not here, for he is risen, as he said
His body had been taken to another tomb
The guards had hidden him in the city
He would remain in the tomb until the fourth day
explanation: The angel said, 'He is not here: for he is risen, as he said. Come, see the place where the Lord lay' (Matthew 28:6).
hint: The angel connects his words to what Jesus himself had said earlier.

clue: Final report: some of the watch went into the city and told the chief priests all that was done. Soon afterward a particular saying was 'commonly reported among the Jews.'
prompt: Case solved: where did the story that the disciples stole the body come from?
options: The chief priests and elders gave the soldiers large money to say the disciples stole him while they slept
The soldiers personally saw the disciples carry the body away
The women told the disciples that the body had been stolen
Pilate announced it after investigating the tomb himself
keywords: stole him away while we slept
explanation: After taking counsel, the chief priests and elders 'gave large money unto the soldiers,' telling them to say 'His disciples came by night, and stole him away while we slept,' and the soldiers 'did as they were taught' (Matthew 28:12-15).
hint: Notice who paid whom, and the phrase 'did as they were taught'.

clue: Trade ledger note: a local craftsman known for making silver shrines for Diana is said to have brought 'no small gain' unto the craftsmen. He called them together with the workmen of like occupation.
prompt: Who called the craftsmen together at the start of the uproar, and what was his trade?
options: Demetrius, a silversmith who made silver shrines for Diana
Alexander, a coppersmith who made idols for Jupiter
Gaius, a tentmaker who sold goods in the market
The townclerk, a scribe who kept the temple records
explanation: Acts 19:24-25 names Demetrius, a silversmith who made silver shrines for Diana, as the man who called together the workmen of like occupation.
hint: Look for the man whose craft brought 'no small gain unto the craftsmen.'

clue: Witness statement from the craftsmen's meeting: 'He told us that by this craft we have our wealth, and that one man had turned away much people, not only at Ephesus but almost throughout all Asia.'
prompt: According to the speech at the meeting, what was Paul saying that put the craft in danger?
options: That the temple of Diana should be torn down by force
That they be no gods, which are made with hands
That the craftsmen were charging unfair prices
That the shrines should be given away rather than sold
explanation: In Acts 19:26-27 the speaker says Paul persuaded many, saying 'they be no gods, which are made with hands,' so that 'this our craft is in danger to be set at nought' and Diana's temple would be despised.
hint: The complaint concerns what is fashioned by human hands.

clue: Scene report: the whole city was filled with confusion. Two of Paul's travel companions from Macedonia were seized, and the crowd rushed with one accord to a public gathering place. Paul's friends urged him not to go in.
prompt: As the crowd rushed with one accord into the theatre, whom did they seize?
options: Paul and Silas
Alexander and Demetrius
Gaius and Aristarchus
Timothy and Erastus
explanation: Acts 19:29 records that the crowd caught Gaius and Aristarchus, men of Macedonia, Paul's companions in travel, and rushed into the theatre. Verses 30-31 add that the disciples and certain of the chief of Asia kept Paul from entering.
hint: The text calls them 'men of Macedonia, Paul's companions in travel.'

clue: Crowd observer's note: 'Some cried one thing, and some another; most did not even know why they had come. A man was put forward to speak and beckoned with his hand, but the moment they learned who he was, they drowned him out.'
prompt: What happened when Alexander tried to make his defence to the people?
options: The crowd listened quietly and then went home
When they knew he was a Jew, they cried out for about two hours, 'Great is Diana of the Ephesians'
Demetrius answered him and the two debated for an hour
He was immediately arrested by the deputies
keywords: Great is Diana of the Ephesians
explanation: Acts 19:33-34 says Alexander beckoned to make his defence, but when the crowd knew he was a Jew, all with one voice cried out for about the space of two hours, 'Great is Diana of the Ephesians.'
hint: Count how long the single chant went on.

clue: Final entry: a city official finally quieted the crowd. He pointed out that the accused men were neither robbers of churches nor blasphemers of the goddess, that the courts were open, and that the city itself risked being called to account for the day's uproar.
prompt: Case solution: who ended the uproar, and how was it resolved?
options: Paul entered the theatre and persuaded the crowd to disperse
Demetrius withdrew his complaint and apologized to the city
The townclerk appeased the people, directed complaints to the law and lawful assembly, and dismissed the assembly
Roman soldiers broke up the crowd and imprisoned Gaius and Aristarchus
explanation: Acts 19:35-41 records that the townclerk appeased the people, said any matter should go to the law, the deputies, or a lawful assembly, warned of being called in question for the uproar, and then dismissed the assembly.
hint: The resolution came from a city official, not from Paul or the craftsmen.

clue: Case note: At daybreak a group gathered and bound themselves under a curse. Their number was counted at more than forty.
prompt: What did the conspirators vow they would not do until they had killed Paul?
options: Neither eat nor drink
Neither sleep nor rest
Neither enter the temple nor pray
Neither leave Jerusalem nor speak to anyone
explanation: Acts 23:12 says they bound themselves under a curse, "saying that they would neither eat nor drink till they had killed Paul," and verse 13 says they were more than forty.
hint: Their oath concerned their daily needs at the table.

clue: Overheard plan: The conspirators went to certain leaders and asked them to pass a request to the chief captain, so Paul would be brought out of the castle.
prompt: What pretext were the leaders to use for having Paul brought down to the council?
options: That Paul had asked to make a public defense
As though they would enquire something more perfectly concerning him
That Paul was to be released to his family
That Paul was to be sent to Rome for trial
explanation: In Acts 23:15 the conspirators told the chief priests and elders to ask that Paul be brought down "as though ye would enquire something more perfectly concerning him," while they waited to kill him before he came near.
hint: The cover story pretended the council wanted more information.

clue: Witness report: A young man entered the castle and told Paul about the men lying in wait. Paul then had a centurion bring him to the chief captain.
prompt: Who was the young man who brought word of the ambush?
options: One of the centurions
A servant of the high priest
Paul's sister's son
One of the forty conspirators
explanation: Acts 23:16 says that "when Paul's sister's son heard of their lying in wait, he went and entered into the castle, and told Paul," and he later repeated the warning to the chief captain privately.
hint: He was a relative of Paul.

clue: Military order: Two centurions were told to make ready two hundred soldiers, threescore and ten horsemen, and two hundred spearmen at the third hour of the night, with beasts provided for Paul.
prompt: Where, and to whom, was Paul to be brought safely?
options: To Rome, to Caesar
To Damascus, to the governor of the city
To Antioch, to the church elders
To Caesarea, to Felix the governor
explanation: Acts 23:23-24 records the order to go to Caesarea and "bring him safe unto Felix the governor."
hint: The destination was a coastal city where a Roman governor sat.

clue: Final report: The soldiers took Paul by night, the horsemen went on with him, and a letter was delivered to the governor along with the prisoner.
prompt: What really happened to Paul after the plot was exposed?
options: He was brought by night to Antipatris, then to Caesarea, and the governor had him kept in Herod's judgment hall until his accusers came
He was handed back to the council, who released him after questioning
He escaped the soldiers and fled to Cilicia
He was killed on the road before reaching the governor
explanation: Acts 23:31-33 says the soldiers brought Paul by night to Antipatris and then presented him to the governor at Caesarea, and verse 35 says the governor would hear him when his accusers came and commanded him to be kept in Herod's judgment hall.
hint: The plot failed, but Paul remained in custody awaiting a hearing.

prompt: According to the parable, when did the enemy come and sow tares among the wheat?
options: While men slept
At the time of harvest
At noon, while the servants watched the field
After the wheat had been gathered into the barn
explanation: Matthew 13:25 says that "while men slept, his enemy came and sowed tares among the wheat, and went his way."
hint: The enemy did his work at a time when no one was watching.

prompt: Why did the householder tell his servants not to gather up the tares right away?
options: Lest they root up also the wheat with them
Because the tares would wither on their own
Because the tares were good to eat
Because the field belonged to the enemy
explanation: In Matthew 13:29 he answered, "Nay; lest while ye gather up the tares, ye root up also the wheat with them."
hint: His concern was for the good crop growing alongside the bad.

prompt: In Jesus' own explanation of the parable, what does the harvest represent?
options: The end of the world
The preaching of John the Baptist
The feast of the Passover
The rebuilding of the temple
keywords: the harvest is the end of the world
explanation: Jesus states in Matthew 13:39 that "the harvest is the end of the world; and the reapers are the angels."
hint: Look at how Jesus identifies the harvest and the reapers together in His explanation.

prompt: Who asked Jesus to explain this parable, and where were they?
options: His disciples, in the house after He sent the multitude away
The Pharisees, in the synagogue
The multitude, on the shore of the sea
The servants of the high priest, in the temple
explanation: Matthew 13:36 records that Jesus "sent the multitude away, and went into the house: and his disciples came unto him, saying, Declare unto us the parable of the tares of the field."
hint: The explanation was given privately, after the crowd had gone.

prompt: When the householder sent his servants to receive the fruits of the vineyard, how did the husbandmen treat them?
options: They beat one, killed another, and stoned another
They paid them half the fruits and sent them away
They welcomed them and gave them all the fruits
They bound them and sent them to the king
explanation: The husbandmen 'took his servants, and beat one, and killed another, and stoned another,' and they treated the next, larger group of servants 'likewise' (Matthew 21:35-36).
hint: The servants received violence, not fruit.

prompt: When the husbandmen saw the householder's son coming, what did they say among themselves?
options: Let us give him the fruits, for he is the lord's son
This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and let us seize on his inheritance
Let us flee into a far country before he comes
Let us send him back to his father with a gift
explanation: Though the father said 'They will reverence my son,' the husbandmen said, 'This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and let us seize on his inheritance,' and they cast him out and slew him (Matthew 21:37-39).
hint: They wanted what would one day belong to the son.

prompt: After quoting the scripture about the stone which the builders rejected, what did Jesus say would happen to the kingdom of God?
options: It would be given to the chief priests as a reward
It would be delayed until the husbandmen repented
It would be taken from them and given to a nation bringing forth the fruits thereof
It would be divided equally among all the husbandmen
explanation: Jesus said, 'The kingdom of God shall be taken from you, and given to a nation bringing forth the fruits thereof' (Matthew 21:43).
hint: Think of what the householder wanted from his vineyard all along.

prompt: When the chief priests and Pharisees perceived that Jesus spoke of them, why did they not lay hands on him at that time?
options: Because the Roman governor forbade it
Because they agreed with the parable and repented
Because it was the sabbath day
Because they feared the multitude, who took him for a prophet
explanation: Though they sought to lay hands on him, 'they feared the multitude, because they took him for a prophet' (Matthew 21:46).
hint: Consider how the crowds around Jesus regarded him.

prompt: What did the father ask his first son to do?
options: Go work to day in his vineyard
Feed the swine in the field
Gather the harvest into his barn
Go up to Jerusalem to pay tribute
explanation: The father came to the first son and said, 'Son, go work to day in my vineyard' (Matthew 21:28).
hint: Think of a place where grapes are grown.

prompt: How did the second son respond when the father gave him the same request?
options: He said, 'I go, sir,' and went not
He said, 'I will not,' but afterward repented and went
He went without saying a word
He asked to take his brother's place
explanation: The second son answered, 'I go, sir: and went not' (Matthew 21:30), the opposite of the first son, who refused but later repented and went (Matthew 21:29).
hint: Compare his words with his actions.

prompt: After his hearers answered that the first son did his father's will, what did Jesus tell them?
options: That the publicans and the harlots go into the kingdom of God before them
That both sons would receive an equal inheritance
That the second son would be cast into outer darkness
That they had answered wrongly
explanation: When they said 'The first,' Jesus replied, 'Verily I say unto you, That the publicans and the harlots go into the kingdom of God before you' (Matthew 21:31).
hint: Jesus names two groups that his religious listeners looked down on.

prompt: In explaining his point, Jesus connected the parable to John. What did he say about how his hearers responded to John?
options: They believed him not, and when they saw others believe, they repented not afterward
They believed him at first but later turned away
They believed him, but the publicans and harlots did not
They never heard John's preaching at all
explanation: Jesus said John came 'in the way of righteousness, and ye believed him not: but the publicans and the harlots believed him,' and even after seeing it they 'repented not afterward' (Matthew 21:32). This ties back to the earlier question about John's baptism (Matthew 21:25).
hint: Recall the counter-question Jesus asked earlier about John's baptism, and who in verse 32 did believe.

prompt: For how long had the owner of the vineyard come seeking fruit on the fig tree without finding any?
options: Three years
Seven years
One year
Twelve years
explanation: The owner told the dresser, 'Behold, these three years I come seeking fruit on this fig tree, and find none' (Luke 13:7).
hint: Look at the owner's complaint to the dresser of his vineyard.

prompt: When the owner ordered the tree cut down, what did the dresser of the vineyard ask to do instead?
options: Let it alone this year also, and dig about it and dung it
Transplant it to a better part of the vineyard
Graft new branches onto it from another tree
Cut it down at once and plant a vine in its place
explanation: The dresser answered, 'Lord, let it alone this year also, till I shall dig about it, and dung it' (Luke 13:8).
hint: He asked for more time and offered to tend the tree himself.

prompt: According to the dresser, what was to happen if the tree still bore no fruit after the extra year of care?
options: It would be cut down
It would be left standing forever
It would be given to another husbandman
It would be burned along with the whole vineyard
explanation: The dresser said, 'if it bear fruit, well: and if not, then after that thou shalt cut it down' (Luke 13:9), so the extra year was a final opportunity, not an endless delay.
hint: The dresser's request had a condition and a deadline.

prompt: Just before this parable, Jesus spoke of the Galilaeans slain by Pilate and the eighteen on whom the tower in Siloam fell. What did he say about them and about his hearers?
options: They were not sinners above others; and except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish
They were sinners above all others, so his hearers had nothing to fear
Such disasters fall only on the wicked, so the righteous need not repent
Their deaths were a sign that the end of the world had come
explanation: Jesus asked whether those victims were sinners above all others and answered, 'I tell you, Nay: but, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish' (Luke 13:3, 5). He then told the parable of the barren fig tree, for which the dresser asked, 'Lord, let it alone this year also' (Luke 13:6-9).
hint: Jesus gave the same answer twice, once for each tragedy.

prompt: At midnight, what does the man ask his friend to lend him?
options: Three loaves
Two fishes
A lamp and oil
A jar of wine
explanation: The man goes at midnight and says, "Friend, lend me three loaves," because a traveling friend has arrived and he has nothing to set before him (Luke 11:5-6).
hint: Think of what a host would need to set before a hungry guest.

prompt: What reason does the friend inside the house give for not getting up?
options: He has no food left in the house
The door is shut and his children are with him in bed
He is too sick to rise
He does not recognize the voice at the door
explanation: He answers from within, "Trouble me not: the door is now shut, and my children are with me in bed; I cannot rise and give thee" (Luke 11:7).
hint: Picture a household already settled down for the night.

prompt: According to Jesus, why does the friend finally rise and give him as many as he needs?
options: Because he is his friend
Because he is paid for the bread
Because of the man's importunity
Because the children wake up hungry
explanation: Jesus says that though he will not rise because he is his friend, "yet because of his importunity he will rise and give him as many as he needeth" (Luke 11:8).
hint: Jesus explicitly rules out friendship as the reason; consider the asker's persistence.

prompt: In his closing comparison with earthly fathers, what does Jesus say the heavenly Father will give to them that ask him?
options: Silver and gold
A sign from heaven
Victory over their enemies
The Holy Spirit
explanation: Jesus reasons that if earthly fathers know how to give good gifts to their children, "how much more shall your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to them that ask him?" (Luke 11:13).
hint: Look at the very last verse of the passage.

parable_title: The Marriage of the King's Son
prompt: When the king's servants announced that the dinner was ready, how did some of the bidden guests respond?
options: They made light of it and went their ways, one to his farm, another to his merchandise
They said they had bought five yoke of oxen and had married a wife
They came to the wedding but left before the dinner was served
They asked the king to postpone the marriage until after the harvest
explanation: Matthew 22:5 says the bidden guests 'made light of it, and went their ways, one to his farm, another to his merchandise,' even after being told all things were ready (Matthew 22:4).
hint: Think of ordinary daily business that pulled them away.

parable_title: The Marriage of the King's Son
prompt: When the king asked a guest how he came in without a wedding garment, how did the man respond?
options: He blamed the servants for bringing him in from the highways
He was speechless
He said he was too poor to buy one
He begged the king for forgiveness
explanation: Matthew 22:12 records the king's question, 'Friend, how camest thou in hither not having a wedding garment?' and states simply, 'And he was speechless.'
hint: The man offered no excuse at all.

parable_title: The Marriage of the King's Son
prompt: With what closing statement does Jesus sum up the parable?
options: So the last shall be first, and the first last
Whosoever exalteth himself shall be abased
For many are called, but few are chosen
The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few
explanation: Jesus ends the parable in Matthew 22:14 with the words, 'For many are called, but few are chosen.'
hint: The saying contrasts an invitation with a selection.

parable_title: The Marriage of the King's Son
prompt: Immediately after this parable, what did the Pharisees do?
options: They believed on Him and were baptized
They went away and held a feast of their own
They asked Him to explain the parable privately
They took counsel how they might entangle Him in His talk
explanation: Matthew 22:15 says, 'Then went the Pharisees, and took counsel how they might entangle him in his talk,' leading to their question about tribute to Caesar.
hint: Read the very next verse after the parable ends; their response was hostile.

parable_title: The Hidden Treasure, the Pearl and the Net
prompt: In the first parable, what did the man do after he found the treasure hid in a field?
options: He hid it, then for joy sold all that he had and bought the field
He dug it up at once and carried it away by night
He reported it to the owner of the field and asked for a reward
He divided it among his neighbours
explanation: Matthew 13:44 says that when the man found the treasure he hid it, and for joy went and sold all that he had and bought that field.
hint: He did not take the treasure right away. Think about what he needed to own first.

parable_title: The Hidden Treasure, the Pearl and the Net
prompt: What did the merchant man, who was seeking goodly pearls, do when he found one pearl of great price?
options: He went and sold all that he had, and bought it
He traded it for many smaller pearls
He gave it to the king as a gift
He left it, because he could not afford it
explanation: Matthew 13:46 says that when the merchant found one pearl of great price, he went and sold all that he had and bought it.
hint: His response is like that of the man in the field.

parable_title: The Hidden Treasure, the Pearl and the Net
prompt: In explaining the parable of the net, whom does Jesus say will come forth at the end of the world to sever the wicked from among the just?
options: The angels
The fishermen of Galilee
The scribes and Pharisees
The disciples
explanation: Jesus says in Matthew 13:49 that at the end of the world the angels shall come forth and sever the wicked from among the just.
hint: Jesus names the ones who do the sorting. They are not human.

parable_title: The Hidden Treasure, the Pearl and the Net
prompt: After asking his disciples whether they had understood all these things, Jesus said that every scribe instructed unto the kingdom of heaven is like what?
options: A householder who brings forth out of his treasure things new and old
A merchant who sells all his pearls for a field
A fisherman who casts away every fish he catches
A man who hides his treasure so that no one may find it
explanation: After the disciples answered 'Yea, Lord,' Jesus said in Matthew 13:52 that every instructed scribe is like a householder who brings forth out of his treasure things new and old.
hint: This picture also involves treasure, but instead of hiding it, the man brings things forth out of it.

prompt: How does Jesus describe the judge in this parable?
options: He feared not God, neither regarded man
He was a righteous man who feared God
He was a priest who served in the temple
He was the widow's own brother
explanation: Luke 18:2 says there was in a city a judge "which feared not God, neither regarded man." He had no reverence for God and no concern for people.
hint: Jesus describes his attitude toward both God and people, and neither is favorable.

prompt: When the judge finally decided to help the widow, what reason did he give within himself?
options: He had come to fear God
He wanted the people of the city to honor him
Her continual coming would weary him
The law of Moses commanded him to do it
explanation: In Luke 18:4-5 the judge admits he fears not God nor regards man, yet says, "because this widow troubleth me, I will avenge her, lest by her continual coming she weary me."
hint: His motive had nothing to do with God or justice; think about her persistence.

prompt: After saying "Hear what the unjust judge saith," what does Jesus declare God will do for his own elect who cry day and night unto him?
options: He will make them wait until they stop asking
He will avenge them speedily
He will give them riches and long life
He will send them to another judge
explanation: In Luke 18:7-8 Jesus asks, "shall not God avenge his own elect, which cry day and night unto him?" and answers, "I tell you that he will avenge them speedily."
hint: Jesus contrasts God with the unjust judge; consider how quickly God acts.

prompt: According to the narrator at the opening of the passage, to what end did Jesus speak this parable?
options: That men ought always to pray, and not to faint
That judges should fear God and regard man
That widows should not go to court
That men should sell all they have and give to the poor
explanation: Luke 18:1 states plainly that Jesus spake this parable "to this end, that men ought always to pray, and not to faint."
hint: Look at the very first verse, before the story itself begins.

prompt: When the supper was prepared, what message did the man send his servant to give to those who had been invited?
options: Come; for all things are now ready.
The supper is delayed until the morning.
Bring a gift worthy of the master's table.
Only the first to arrive may enter.
explanation: The servant was sent at supper time to tell the invited guests, "Come; for all things are now ready" (Luke 14:17).
hint: The invitation stressed that nothing was left to prepare.

prompt: One invited guest did not even ask to be excused but simply said, "I cannot come." What reason did he give?
options: He had bought a piece of ground and had to go see it.
He had married a wife.
He had bought five yoke of oxen to prove them.
He had to bury his father.
explanation: The third guest said, "I have married a wife, and therefore I cannot come" (Luke 14:20), unlike the first two who asked to be excused.
hint: His excuse concerned a new household, not property or livestock.

prompt: How does the story close, stating what will happen to the men who were first invited?
options: They will be given seats of honour when they finally arrive.
They will be invited again to a second supper.
None of them shall taste of his supper.
They must pay for the food that was prepared.
explanation: After the lord orders his servant to compel guests from the highways and hedges so that his house may be filled, the story closes: "none of those men which were bidden shall taste of my supper" (Luke 14:24).
hint: Think about what the refusers lose by turning down the invitation.

prompt: In the parable the master sends for the poor, the maimed, the halt, and the blind. Just before the parable, what had Jesus told his host to do with a similar list of people?
options: Give them alms at the door but not seat them.
Call them when making a feast, for they cannot recompense him.
Send them away so that friends and rich neighbours may come.
Seat them in the lowest room at the table.
explanation: Jesus told the one who bade him, "when thou makest a feast, call the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind," adding that he would be blessed because they cannot recompense him (Luke 14:13-14).
hint: Read the advice Jesus gave to the man who had invited him, just before verse 15.

prompt: In Jesus' story, how much did the two debtors owe the creditor?
options: One owed five hundred pence, and the other fifty
One owed a thousand talents, and the other a hundred
Each owed fifty pence
One owed ten pence, and the other one pence
explanation: Jesus said a certain creditor had two debtors: 'the one owed five hundred pence, and the other fifty' (Luke 7:41).
hint: The larger debt was ten times the smaller one.

prompt: When neither debtor had anything to pay, what did the creditor do?
options: He cast them both into prison
He forgave only the one who owed less
He frankly forgave them both
He gave them more time and demanded interest
explanation: Luke 7:42 says, 'when they had nothing to pay, he frankly forgave them both.'
hint: The creditor treated both debtors the same way.

prompt: Jesus asked Simon which debtor would love the creditor most. What did Simon answer, which Jesus said was rightly judged?
options: The one who had been forgiven least
Neither, since debts cannot produce love
Both would love him equally
The one to whom he forgave most
explanation: Simon answered, 'I suppose that he, to whom he forgave most,' and Jesus replied, 'Thou hast rightly judged' (Luke 7:43).
hint: Think about the size of each debt that was cancelled.

prompt: Turning to the woman, Jesus contrasted her actions with Simon's. Which courtesy did Jesus say Simon had not given Him when He entered the house?
options: He gave no bread for the meal
He gave no water for His feet
He gave no seat at the table
He gave no wine to drink
explanation: Jesus told Simon, 'thou gavest me no water for my feet: but she hath washed my feet with tears,' and likewise noted Simon gave no kiss and no oil (Luke 7:44-46).
hint: The woman supplied this lack with her tears.
